content: Does newborn screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) lead to better clinical outcomes, improved quality of life, and increased survival rates? This study aimed to determine whether newborn screening for CF can prevent or reduce irreversible organ damage and improve clinical outcomes, quality of life, and survival, without causing unacceptable adverse effects. To address this question, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register. This register includes references from electronic database searches, handsearches of relevant journals, and conference proceedings. The last search of the register was performed in June 2008. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials, both published and unpublished, that compared newborn screening to clinical diagnosis in individuals with CF. Two authors independently assessed the eligibility and quality of the trials and extracted data. Allocation concealment was unclear in both studies, but sequence generation was deemed adequate in one of them. The search identified six trials, but only two trials met the inclusion criteria. These two trials involved a total of 1,124,483 neonates, of whom 210 were diagnosed with CF. The maximum follow-up period for these studies was 17 years. Due to differences in study designs, reported outcomes, and summary measures, it was not possible to calculate pooled estimates. Data from only one study were analyzed in detail. The results showed that severe malnutrition was less common among participants who underwent newborn screening. In the control group, the odds of having a weight below the tenth percentile were 4.12 times higher (95% CI 1.64 to 10.38), and the odds of having a height below the tenth percentile were 4.62 times higher (95% CI 1.69 to 12.61) compared to the screened group. By the age of seven, 88% of screened participants and 75% of controls had lung function parameters within normal limits (defined as at least 89% of predicted values). At the time of diagnosis, chest radiograph scores were significantly better in the screened group. Specifically, 33% of screened participants had Wisconsin chest X-ray (WCXR) scores over five, compared to 50% in the control group (P = 0.097). Similarly, 24% of screened participants had Brasfield chest X-ray (BCXR) scores under 21, compared to 45% in the control group (P = 0.042). However, over time, chest radiograph scores worsened in the screened group (WCXR P = 0.017 and BCXR P = 0.041). After adjusting for confounding factors such as genotype, pancreatic status, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonization, these results were no longer statistically significant. In the screened group, colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa occurred earlier. However, estimates suggest that diagnosing CF through newborn screening is less expensive than traditional clinical diagnosis. In conclusion, two randomized controlled trials evaluating newborn screening for CF were identified, and data from one study were included in the analysis. Nutritional benefits were evident in the screened group. While screening has the potential to improve pulmonary outcomes, long-term pulmonary prognosis was influenced by confounding factors. Additionally, newborn screening appears to be more cost-effective than traditional diagnostic methods.
